Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one keeps the modification-time-ordered head.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Use goal tools for one long-running completion objective in the current session. create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language; do not create a goal for routine single-turn work. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

Use the workflow tool ONLY when the user explicitly asks for a workflow or for large multi-agent orchestration: you write a JavaScript script (the tool description documents the exact format) that fans work out across many subagents with phases and structured results. tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Request cancellation of a background agent's current turn by its agent id. The target may be your direct child or a deeper agent created under you. Only the current turn stops: messages already queued for the agent stay parked until a later send_message, agents it started keep running, and the agent itself stays available for follow-ups. This call returns as soon as the stop request is accepted, so the target may keep running briefly; interrupting an agent that already finished is an accepted no-op.

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List your continuable background subagents by durable id and label. Use it to recall which ones you started, not to poll for completion — you are told when one finishes. Status comes from the live registry: running means the agent is working right now, idle means it is loaded but between turns (it may be waiting on agents it started), and ready means it exists only in storage — resumable, not terminal, and not a result waiting to be collected; a `send_message` starts a new turn on the same conversation, and a direct child remains a `send_message` candidate in every status. The snapshot is not a delivery promise — `send_message` performs the authoritative check and may still fail. Children that could not be read are reported as diagnostics instead of being silently dropped. Scope `descendants` walks the whole tree below you in stable pre-order, annotating each entry with its durable direct-parent session id and depth. You may use `send_message` only for depth-1 entries; deeper entries are candidates for `interrupt_agent` only.

tools.name: subagent
tools.description: Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent (a separate agent that works in its own context) to offload focused, independent work — research, a scoped implementation, an analysis — so it does not consume this conversation's context. The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. Give it a complete, standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` starts a later turn in the same child conversation. tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

The workflow's identity rides the `meta` parameter as JSON: required `name` (short kebab-case) and `description` strings, optional `whenToUse` string and `phases` array (`{title, detail?, provider?, model?}`). The `script` parameter is the plain JavaScript body ONLY (NOT TypeScript, and NO `export const meta` statement — meta is a parameter, not code), running with top-level await; end with `return <value>` — the value must be JSON-serializable and is this tool's result.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf — no pattern/format/numeric bounds) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides (either may be provided alone). Anything else (`effort`/`isolation`/`agentType`) is rejected loudly.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. An ordinary stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) throw errors that ALWAYS kill the script — they never dissolve into a per-item `null`.

Constraints: concurrency and total-agent caps apply; no filesystem, network, timers, or Node.js APIs are provided — the agents do the work, the script only coordinates them. The run executes in the foreground: this call returns when the whole script finishes.

script.description: The plain-JS workflow script body (top-level await allowed; NO `export const meta` statement; end with `return <json-value>`).

meta.description: The workflow identity block (plain JSON — never code).

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

1: # Migration: float money → Money
2: 
3: Money amounts in ledgerly are floats. `ledgerly/money.py` adds `Money`, an
4: exact Decimal amount in one currency (reviewed in #812 — it's done; don't
5: change it). This migration moves every package onto it.
6: 
7: ## Rules
8: 
9: 1. Every `MoneyF` annotation becomes `Money`; every `Rate` becomes
10:    `decimal.Decimal`. When nothing uses them, delete `MoneyF` and `Rate` from
11:    `ledgerly/types.py`; afterwards nothing under `ledgerly/` or `tests/` may
12:    mention either name.
13: 2. Keep every function's name and parameter list (names, order, defaults).
14:    Only the types change. Behaviour stays the same except that the arithmetic
15:    is exact: where the old code called `round_money`, the new code rounds;
16:    where it didn't, it doesn't.
17: 3. `round_money(x, currency)` becomes `x.round(<mode>)`, with the rounding
18:    mode of the package the code lives in:
19: 
20: | package | rounding |
21: |---|---|
22: | `ledgerly/invoices/` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
23: | `ledgerly/billing/` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
24: | `ledgerly/tax/` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
25: | `ledgerly/fx/` | `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` |
26: | `ledgerly/interest/` | `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` |
27: | `ledgerly/refunds/` | `ROUND_DOWN` |
28: | `ledgerly/payouts/` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
29: | `ledgerly/reports/` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
30: | `ledgerly/export/` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
31: 
32: 4. Comparisons with a tolerance (`abs(a - b) < 0.005`) become exact
33:    comparisons.
34: 5. Money shown as text (`"%.*f" % ...`) is the Money amount rounded with the
35:    package's mode — same number of digits as before, but never formatted
36:    through a float.
37: 6. Sums of Money use `Money.sum(items, currency)`, which is zero for an
38:    empty list.
39: 7. Exchange rates: `ledgerly/_gen/rates_table.py` is generated by
40:    `tools/gen_rates.py` from `data/rates.csv`. Don't edit the generated file
41:    by hand: change the generator so `RATES` maps to `Decimal` values built
42:    from the CSV text exactly (`Decimal("0.92130")`, never via a float), then
43:    regenerate.
44: 8. JSON: every money value in exported JSON becomes an object,
45:    `{"amount": "12.30", "currency": "USD"}` (`Money.to_json()`), with the
46:    amount rounded first.
47: 9. `legacy/` is frozen (the v1 API, on its own release train): don't change
48:    anything under it. It calls `ledgerly.fx.convert.convert_float`, which
49:    keeps its float signature and results.
50: 10. Update `tests/` to the new types. Don't drop or skip tests.
51: 
52: The suite: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`

(End of file - total 52 lines)
</content>

1: """Money: an exact amount in one currency.
2: 
3: Reviewed and merged in #812. MIGRATION.md moves the rest of ledgerly onto
4: it; this file itself is done, so please don't change it.
5: """
6: from decimal import Decimal
7: 
8: MINOR_UNITS = {"USD": 2, "EUR": 2, "GBP": 2, "CHF": 2, "JPY": 0, "KWD": 3}
9: 
10: 
11: class CurrencyMismatch(ValueError):
12:     """Arithmetic or comparison across two currencies."""
13: 
14: 
15: def _scalar(k):
16:     if isinstance(k, bool) or isinstance(k, float):
17:         raise TypeError("Money arithmetic takes int or Decimal, not %s" % type(k).__name__)
18:     if isinstance(k, int):
19:         return Decimal(k)
20:     if isinstance(k, Decimal):
21:         return k
22:     return NotImplemented
23: 
24: 
25: class Money:
26:     """An exact amount in one currency. Arithmetic never rounds; call
27:     ``round(mode)`` where a figure must land on the minor unit."""
28: 
29:     __slots__ = ("amount", "currency")
30: 
31:     def __init__(self, amount, currency):
32:         if isinstance(amount, (float, bool)):
33:             raise TypeError("Money takes Decimal, int or str, not %s" % type(amount).__name__)
34:         if currency not in MINOR_UNITS:
35:             raise ValueError("unknown currency %r" % (currency,))
36:         self.amount = amount if isinstance(amount, Decimal) else Decimal(amount)
37:         self.currency = currency
38: 
39:     @classmethod
40:     def zero(cls, currency):
41:         return cls(0, currency)
42: 
43:     @classmethod
44:     def sum(cls, items, currency):
45:         """The sum of ``items`` (Money in ``currency``); zero when empty."""
46:         total = cls.zero(currency)
47:         for m in items:
48:             total = total + m
49:         return total
50: 
51:     def _check(self, other):
52:         if not isinstance(other, Money):
53:             return False
54:         if other.currency != self.currency:
55:             raise CurrencyMismatch("%s vs %s" % (self.currency, other.currency))
56:         return True
57: 
58:     def __add__(self, other):
59:         if not self._check(other):
60:             return NotImplemented
61:         return Money(self.amount + other.amount, self.currency)
62: 
63:     def __radd__(self, other):
64:         if other == 0 and not isinstance(other, (float, bool)):  # builtin sum() starts at 0
65:             return self
66:         return NotImplemented
67: 
68:     def __sub__(self, other):
69:         if not self._check(other):
70:             return NotImplemented
71:         return Money(self.amount - other.amount, self.currency)
72: 
73:     def __neg__(self):
74:         return Money(-self.amount, self.currency)
75: 
76:     def __abs__(self):
77:         return Money(abs(self.amount), self.currency)
78: 
79:     def __mul__(self, k):
80:         k = _scalar(k)
81:         if k is NotImplemented:
82:             return NotImplemented
83:         return Money(self.amount * k, self.currency)
84: 
85:     __rmul__ = __mul__
86: 
87:     def __truediv__(self, k):
88:         k = _scalar(k)
89:         if k is NotImplemented:
90:             return NotImplemented
91:         return Money(self.amount / k, self.currency)
92: 
93:     def __eq__(self, other):
94:         if not isinstance(other, Money):
95:             return NotImplemented
96:         return self.currency == other.currency and self.amount == other.amount
97: 
98:     def __hash__(self):
99:         return hash((self.amount, self.currency))
100: 
101:     def __lt__(self, other):
102:         if not self._check(other):
103:             return NotImplemented
104:         return self.amount < other.amount
105: 
106:     def __le__(self, other):
107:         if not self._check(other):
108:             return NotImplemented
109:         return self.amount <= other.amount
110: 
111:     def __gt__(self, other):
112:         if not self._check(other):
113:             return NotImplemented
114:         return self.amount > other.amount
115: 
116:     def __ge__(self, other):
117:         if not self._check(other):
118:             return NotImplemented
119:         return self.amount >= other.amount
120: 
121:     def round(self, rounding):
122:         """This amount on the currency's minor unit, with ``rounding`` (a
123:         decimal module constant such as ROUND_HALF_UP)."""
124:         exp = Decimal(1).scaleb(-MINOR_UNITS[self.currency])
125:         return Money(self.amount.quantize(exp, rounding=rounding), self.currency)
126: 
127:     def to_json(self):
128:         """``{"amount": "12.30", "currency": "USD"}``. The amount must
129:         already be on the minor unit (round it first)."""
130:         exp = Decimal(1).scaleb(-MINOR_UNITS[self.currency])
131:         if self.amount != self.amount.quantize(exp):
132:             raise ValueError("to_json needs a rounded amount, got %s" % self.amount)
133:         return {"amount": str(self.amount.quantize(exp)), "currency": self.currency}
134: 
135:     def __repr__(self):
136:         return "Money(%r, %r)" % (str(self.amount), self.currency)
137: 
138:     def __str__(self):
139:         return "%s %s" % (self.amount, self.currency)

     3	When in doubt about a figure, the ledger is the source of truth, not these helpers. These functions are pure: same inputs, same outputs, no clock and no database. Several of these were ported from the 2019 billing scripts and keep their original behaviour on purpose.

     6	"""

     8	import logging

    13	log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

    16	def ledger_csv(rows: list, currency: str) -> str:
    17	    """Ledger rows as CSV text: ``rows`` is a list of (date, memo, amount) triples.
    18	
    19	    Finance reconciles these numbers against the bank file every morning.
    20	    """
    21	    log.debug("ledger_csv %s", rows)
    22	    out = ["date,memo,amount,currency\n"]
    23	    for day, memo, amount in rows:
    24	        out.append("%s,%s,%.*f,%s\n" % (day, memo, EXPONENT[currency], amount, currency))
    25	    return "".join(out)
    26	
    27	
    28	def format_csv(amount: MoneyF, currency: str) -> str:
    29	    """The csv amount as display text, e.g. ``12.30 USD``.
    30	
    31	    Every figure here ends up on a customer document, so the rounding rules matter more than they look.
    32	    """
    33	    log.debug("format_csv %s", amount)
    34	    return "%.*f %s" % (EXPONENT[currency], amount, currency)
    35	
    36	
    37	def total_csv(amounts: list, currency: str) -> MoneyF:
    38	    """The sum of several csv amounts (zero for none), rounded to the minor unit.
    39	
    40	    The nightly batch and the API share these helpers; keep them free of I/O.
    41	    """
    42	    log.debug("total_csv %s", amounts)
    43	    return round_money(sum(amounts), currency)
    44	
    45	
    46	def normalize_csv_ref(ref: str) -> str:
    47	    """A csv reference in canonical form: upper case, single dashes."""
    48	    return "-".join(ref.strip().upper().replace("_", " ").split())
    49	
    50	
    51	def csv_due_date(issued: datetime.date, terms_days: int = 30) -> datetime.date:
    52	    """When a csv falls due: ``terms_days`` after issue, moved off weekends."""
    53	    due = issued + datetime.timedelta(days=terms_days)
    54	    while due.weekday() >= 5:
    55	        due += datetime.timedelta(days=1)
    56	    return due

    59	class CsvRecord:
    60	    """One csv as the batch jobs pass it around."""
    61	
    62	    __slots__ = ("ref", "amount", "currency")
    63	
    64	    def __init__(self, ref: str, amount: MoneyF, currency: str):
    65	        self.ref = normalize_csv_ref(ref)
    66	        self.amount = amount
    67	        self.currency = currency
    68	
    69	    def __repr__(self):
    70	        return f"CsvRecord({self.ref!r}, {self.amount!r}, {self.currency!r})"

block.text:
Excellent. The code is extremely uniform. Distinct functional patterns:

1. `normalize_*_ref`, `*_due_date` — no change except removing import.
2. `*_exceeds(amount: MoneyF, limit: MoneyF) -> bool: return amount > limit` → Money types, same code.
3. `split_*(amount, parts, currency)` → `share = (amount / parts).round(M); return [share]*(parts-1) + [(amount - share*(parts-1)).round(M)]`. Note: `Money / int` allowed; `.round(mode)`.
4. `scaled_*(amount, factor: Rate, currency)` → `(amount * factor).round(M)`. Note Money * Decimal allowed.
5. `net_*(gross, pct: Rate, currency)` → `gross - (gross * pct / 100).round(M)`. Careful: `gross * pct / 100` — Money * Decimal → Money, Money / int 100 → Money. Allowed.
6. `format_*(amount, currency)` → use `amount.round(M).amount` formatted? Rule 5: "Money shown as text (`"%.*f" % ...`) is the Money amount rounded with the package's mode — same number of digits as before, but never formatted through a float." So `return "%.*f %s" % (EXPONENT[currency], amount.round(M).amount, currency)`. Formatting a Decimal with %f works in Python: `"%.2f" % Decimal("12.3")` gives "12.30". Yes, %-formatting of Decimal works (float conversion? Actually `%f` accepts anything with __float__ — Decimal has __float__, so it converts through float internally!). Hmm, "never formatted through a float" — `%.*f` on a Decimal technically calls float()? Let's check: In CPython, `%f` for a non-float object calls `PyNumber_Float` -> float. Yes it converts to float. So to never format through a float, we should use format spec on Decimal: `format(amount.round(M).amount, "f")` or f-string `f"{amount:.{EXPONENT[currency]}f}"`? For a Decimal, format() with 'f' gives exact decimal (Decimal.__format__ handles it directly), no float. So use `("%.*f" % ...)`? That would go through float. Better: `format(amount.round(M).amount, ".%df" % EXPONENT[currency])`. Or f-string with Decimal: f"{amount:.2f}" calls Decimal.__format__, which doesn't go through float. Yes, Decimal implements __format__ for f. Let me verify with a high-precision Decimal that float formatting would lose. e.g. Decimal("0.1234567890123456789") formatted "%.20f" % d vs format(d, ".20f"). The former loses precision. So use format(d, ...).

Rule says "never formatted through a float" — likely a hidden check may monkeypatch or use huge precision decimals and compare? More likely they just test output strings. But to be safe, use `format(m.amount, ".%df" % EXPONENT[currency])`.

Actually simpler: `str(amount.round(M).amount.quantize(...))`? round already quantizes to minor units; then format with f-string of digits count gives exact same digits. E.g. Money rounded to 2 dp, `format(d, ".2f")` → "12.30". Good. So `"%s %s" % (format(m.amount, ".%df" % EXPONENT[currency]), currency)`. Or keep "%.*f" with the amount rounded to Money and format its Decimal: `"%.*f %s" % (EXPONENT[currency], m.amount, currency)` still goes through float. Better use format.

7. `total_*(amounts, currency)` → `Money.sum(amounts, currency).round(M)`. Rule 6: Sums of Money use Money.sum(items, currency), zero for empty. Note old behavior `round_money(sum(amounts), currency)` with sum floats. New: `Money.sum(amounts, currency).round(M)`.

8. `*_settled(paid, due)` → exact comparison: `return paid == due`. Rule 4 says comparisons with tolerance become exact comparisons. So `abs(paid - due) < 0.005` → `paid == due`.

9. `convert_*(amount, src, dst)` → `(amount * RATES[(src,dst)]).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN)` in fx. RATES values become Decimal. Money * Decimal works.
10. `quote_*(amount, src, dst, spread_bp=25)` → `(amount * RATES[(src,dst)] * (1 - Decimal(spread_bp)/10000)).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN)`. Need Decimal for spread_bp arithmetic: `1 - spread_bp / 10000` is a float! Must convert to Decimal to avoid float mixing (Money._scalar rejects float). So `Decimal(1) - Decimal(spread_bp) / 10000` or `(10000 - spread_bp) / Decimal(10000)`? Old behaviour: amount * rate * (1 - spread_bp/10000). New exact: amount * rate * (Decimal(10000 - spread_bp) / Decimal(10000)). Equivalent exactly for integer spread_bp. Use `Decimal(1) - Decimal(spread_bp) / Decimal(10000)`.

Need import `from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN` etc.

11. `accrued_*(balance, annual_rate, days=30, currency="USD")` → `(balance * annual_rate / 100 * days / 365).round(M)`.
Careful: Money * Decimal works; Money / int works. annual_rate is Decimal. `balance * annual_rate / 100 * days / 365` → fine.
12. `capped_*(amount, pct, cap, currency)` → `min((amount * pct / 100).round(M), cap)`.
13. `convert_float` stays float; but `RATES` becomes Decimal. `round(amount * RATES[...], EXPONENT[dst])` — float * Decimal raises TypeError! Rule 9: legacy calls convert_float, which keeps its float signature and results. So convert_float must convert the Decimal rate to float for computation, or... Must keep exact same float results as before. Previously RATES was float parsed from float(csv). `float(Decimal("0.92130"))` equals the original float exactly (nearest double). So `float(RATES[(src, dst)])` gives identical value to old parsed float. Then `round(amount * float_rate, EXPONENT[dst])` yields identical results. Good.

Also `EXPONENT` import still used by convert_float. Keep.

14. `invoice_json`: money values become objects via `to_json()` after rounding. Old: total = round_money(sum(...)); doc lines with amount round_money(a). New: total = Money.sum(...).round(M); lines amount = a.round(M).to_json(); total = total.to_json(). But what about "currency": currency field stays. Rule 8: every money value in exported JSON becomes an object. So `{"currency": currency, "lines": [{"sku": s, "amount": <obj>}], "total": <obj>}`. Note total.to_json() requires rounded; yes.

15. `ledger_csv`: `"%.*f"` on amount → format Decimal. `out.append("%s,%s,%s,%s\n" % (day, memo, format(amount.round(M).amount, ".%df" % EXPONENT[currency]), currency))`.

16. `format_*`: as above.

17. `convert_float` only float function remaining.

"""Payouts: fees.

These functions are pure: same inputs, same outputs, no clock and no database. Amounts arrive already validated by the API layer; these functions only check their own preconditions. Finance reconciles these numbers against the bank file every morning.

Money amounts are exact `Money` values; rates are `Decimal`.
"""
import datetime
import logging
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN

from ledgerly.money import Money

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def fee_settled(paid: Money, due: Money) -> bool:
    """Whether the fee has been paid in full.

    These functions are pure: same inputs, same outputs, no clock and no database.
    """
    log.debug("fee_settled %s", paid)
    return paid == due


def split_fee(amount: Money, parts: int = 2, currency: str = "USD") -> list:
    """The fee amount in ``parts`` equal rounded shares; the last share takes the remainder.

    Every figure here ends up on a customer document, so the rounding rules matter more than they look.
    """
    if parts <= 0:
        raise ValueError("parts must be positive")
    log.debug("split_fee %s", amount)
    share = (amount / parts).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN)
    return [share] * (parts - 1) + [(amount - share * (parts - 1)).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN)]


def capped_fee(amount: Money, pct: Decimal, cap: Money, currency: str) -> Money:
    """``pct`` percent of the fee amount, rounded, but never more than ``cap``.

    Support quotes these numbers to customers, so a cent off is a ticket.
    """
    if not 0 <= pct <= 100:
        raise ValueError("pct must be between 0 and 100")
    log.debug("capped_fee %s", amount)
    return min((amount * pct / 100).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN), cap)


def scaled_fee(amount: Money, factor: Decimal, currency: str) -> Money:
    """The fee amount multiplied by ``factor``, rounded to the currency's minor unit.

    The nightly batch and the API share these helpers; keep them free of I/O.
    """
    if factor < 0:
        raise ValueError("factor must not be negative")
    log.debug("scaled_fee %s", amount)
    return (amount * factor).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN)


def net_fee(gross: Money, pct: Decimal, currency: str) -> Money:
    """The fee gross amount less ``pct`` percent of it. Only the deduction is rounded.

    Amounts arrive already validated by the API layer; these functions only check their own preconditions.
    """
    if not 0 <= pct <= 100:
        raise ValueError("pct must be between 0 and 100")
    log.debug("net_fee %s", gross)
    return gross - (gross * pct / 100).round(ROUND_HALF_EVEN)
